newsitem.title: CROATIA: Zagreb readies war criminal list in Serb zone.
newsitem.headline: Zagreb readies war criminal list in Serb zone.

text.p: Croatia promised on Monday to issue a precise list of wanted war criminals presumed living in the Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia, a move meant to ease fear over the region's pending return to central government rule.

Eastern Slavonia is due to be reintegrated in Croatia soon after April elections in a peaceful end to an ethnic conflict that started in 1991 when minority Serbs opposing Croatia's independence from Yugoslavia carved out their own mini-state.
Zagreb recaptured two breakaway Serb enclaves in 1995 and established diplomatic ties with the rebels' backer Yugoslavia.
It also agreed to reintegrate Eastern Slavonia peacefully, in part by amnestying all Serbs who took part in the rebellion except those accused of war atrocities.

"One of these days the final list of war criminals will be known, so the rest of the population (in the enclave) can be at ease, as there will be no revenge. Those are further guarantees from our president," deputy Prime Minister Ivica Kostovic said.
He spoke after talks between President Franjo Tudjman and Eastern Slavonian Serb leader Vojislav Stanimirovic and the enclave's U.N. transitional administrator, Jacques Klein.

A prominent Serb official in the enclave told Reuters last week that Croatia's amnesty law for Serbs, enacted under Western pressure last year, was being "manipulated and does not include all the persons it should".
"We need a precise list of names with evidence that they committed war crimes," said Vojin Susa, the East Slavonian Serbs' negotiator for justice issues.

Klein agreed. "We need this final amnesty list so that people in the region can be reassured and know those who are and those who are not (on the list)," said Klein, head of the 5,000-strong U.N. mission whose mandate expires on July 15.

Many Serbs in the region have reluctantly agreed to live under Croatian rule but fear that human and minority rights granted by Zagreb will not be observed on the ground once Croatian refugees driven out in 1991 start returning.

"We have to keep reassuring them (Serbs) there will be no revenge, that they really do have a future here and there is no reason to leave," Klein said, referring to recent reports of Serb families leaving for Yugoslavia or Serb-held Bosnia.

"We know quite a few people are leaving and taking all their goods with them. We are trying to put a stop to it with concrete measures and I believe the amnesty will have a positive effect," Stanimirovic told reporters.

In another positive sign, Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic will visit the Yugoslav capital Belgrade on Wednesday for talks which, Klein said, could solidify the process of Eastern Slavonia's reintegration.
"That's very important for us as ... the whole process (of reintegration) is very much tied to mutual relations that Zagreb and Belgrade have," Klein told reporters.
